explanations.explanation: Asaph, the psalm's writer, doesn't pretend to be fine. In verse 2 he says, "my soul refused to be comforted." He's honest with God about how heavy the day is. I think that honesty is worth noticing, friend.
Nope, no quick fix here. Asaph, the psalm's writer, isn't rushing through his hurt. In verse 2 he says, "my soul refused to be comforted." Some days are slow like that, and the psalm lets him say so.

Sleep never shows up as a comfort in this verse. What the text says is that Asaph's hands stayed outstretched through the night and "my soul refused to be comforted." Sleep is actually going to be a problem a few verses later. Hang on to that thought.

explanations.answer: He groans and his spirit grows faint
explanations.explanation: Asaph, the psalm's writer, tells it like it is in verse 3: "I remembered You, O God, and I groaned; I mused and my spirit grew faint." Thinking of God didn't give him a quick lift in that moment. That's a man being real in a hard night.

explanations.answer: He sings and his spirit grows strong
explanations.explanation: Not that one, friend. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 3, "I remembered You, O God, and I groaned; I mused and my spirit grew faint." Singing and strength aren't what the verse says. He's still in the low part here.

explanations.answer: He rests and his spirit grows calm
explanations.explanation: No rest yet. Verse 3 says he groaned and his spirit "grew faint." Calm is not what Asaph is feeling right now, and he doesn't dress it up. It gets even less restful in the next verse.
Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 4, "I am too troubled to speak." I think he's so weighed down that the words just won't come. The verse also says his eyes won't close. That's a rough combo.
Angry is a good guess, but the psalm doesn't say it. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 4, "I am too troubled to speak." Troubled is the word he picks, so that's the one we keep.
Proud doesn't fit here at all. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 4, "I am too troubled to speak." He isn't strutting around. I think he's carrying a heavy heart.

Asaph, the psalm's writer, says his spirit pondered at night, and in verse 7 it asks, "Will the Lord spurn us forever and never show His favor again?" Spurn means push away. I think it's brave to ask a question like that. He's asking, not deciding.

explanations.answer: His own nights without any sleep
explanations.explanation: His eyes not closing is in verse 4, but that's not what this question is about. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says his spirit pondered, "Will the Lord spurn us forever and never show His favor again?" Notice the word "us." I think he's thinking about God's people, not just himself.

Wars never come up in these questions. Verse 7 asks, "Will the Lord spurn us forever and never show His favor again?" It's all about how the Lord treats His people. Asaph keeps his eyes on that one worry.
True. Verse 8 asks, "Is His loving devotion gone forever? Has His promise failed for all time?" Those are questions, not conclusions. Asaph lays them out honestly, and the psalm lets him.

Actually, it's true. Verse 8 says, "Is His loving devotion gone forever? Has His promise failed for all time?" It's a pile of hard questions, and Asaph doesn't tiptoe around them. The text records every one.
Verse 9 asks, "Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has His anger shut off His compassion?" Compassion is the word. Asaph is asking the question, not stating it as fact. Big difference, friend.
Power isn't the worry in this verse. Asaph asks, "Has His anger shut off His compassion?" It's about whether God's kindness is still open. Power gets its turn later in the psalm.
Wisdom doesn't make the list here. Asaph, the psalm's writer, asks, "Has His anger shut off His compassion?" I think his worry is about God's tenderness toward His people. That's the one on his mind.

explanations.answer: The right hand of the Most High
explanations.explanation: Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 10, "I am grieved that the right hand of the Most High has changed." He says he's grieved. That's his own sorrow talking, and he says it straight. Then the next verse turns the whole psalm around.

explanations.answer: The hearts of the people of Israel
explanations.explanation: The people's hearts aren't the subject here. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 10, "I am grieved that the right hand of the Most High has changed." He's pointing at God's right hand, not at the people. He says it as his grief, so we let him say it.

explanations.answer: The song he sang in the night
explanations.explanation: His song is mentioned in verse 6, but it isn't what Asaph, the psalm's writer, says has changed. In verse 10 he says, "I am grieved that the right hand of the Most High has changed." The right hand is what's on his heart. Good try on the song, though.

Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 11, "I will remember the works of the LORD; yes, I will remember Your wonders of old." See that turn? He goes from asking questions to choosing what to remember. I think that's the moment the whole psalm swings.
Sins never come up in this verse. Asaph says, "I will remember the works of the LORD; yes, I will remember Your wonders of old." He sets his mind on what the LORD has done. That's the whole decision.

Enemies aren't in this psalm at all, friend. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 11, "I will remember the works of the LORD; yes, I will remember Your wonders of old." He looks at the LORD's works, not at anybody's schemes.

Not quite, baker. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 12, "I will reflect on all You have done and ponder Your mighty deeds." Reflect and ponder are not quick-glance words. He plans to sit with it.
False is right. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 12, "I will reflect on all You have done and ponder Your mighty deeds." That's slow, careful thinking. He isn't skimming, he's settling in.

explanations.answer: What god is so great as our God
explanations.explanation: Verse 13 says, "Your way, O God, is holy. What god is so great as our God?" Asaph asks it right after calling God's way holy. The question is a way of saying nobody compares. Nice and clear.

explanations.answer: How long will this night go on
explanations.explanation: That sounds like the old Asaph from the first half. Verse 13 says, "Your way, O God, is holy. What god is so great as our God?" The night talk has moved on. Now he's looking at who God is.

explanations.answer: Who can stand before our God
explanations.explanation: That's a fair-sounding question, but it's not in this verse. Verse 13 says, "What god is so great as our God?" It's right after "Your way, O God, is holy." Keep an eye on that exact wording.

explanations.answer: The sons of Jacob and Joseph
explanations.explanation: Verse 15 says, "With power You redeemed Your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph." Those are God's own people. Asaph names them by their family line, and that's the answer.

explanations.answer: The sons of Moab and Ammon
explanations.explanation: Moab and Ammon aren't the ones named here. Verse 15 says God redeemed "…Your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph." Asaph is talking about God's own people, so those other names don't fit.

explanations.answer: The sons of Esau and Ishmael
explanations.explanation: Those names aren't the ones in the verse. Verse 15 says, "…Your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph." Those are the people God redeemed with power. Esau and Ishmael just aren't in this psalm.

explanations.answer: They swirl and even the depths shake
explanations.explanation: Verse 16 says, "The waters saw You, O God; the waters saw You and swirled; even the depths were shaken." Even the deepest parts got shaken. If I felt that, I'd hold onto my hat, and my gold base too.

explanations.answer: They freeze and the depths stand still
explanations.explanation: Opposite direction, friend. Verse 16 says the waters "…swirled; even the depths were shaken." Nothing stands still here. The waters are moving the moment they see God.

explanations.answer: They rise and cover the whole land
explanations.explanation: Flooding the land isn't in this verse. It says, "the waters saw You and swirled; even the depths were shaken." The picture is swirling and shaking, not rising up over everything. Good to read it exactly.

Not a chance, baker. Verse 18 says, "the earth trembled and quaked." With thunder in the whirlwind and lightning lighting up the world, nothing is sitting perfectly still. That's one very shaky ground.
False, and the text is loud about it. Verse 18 says, "Your thunder resounded in the whirlwind; the lightning lit up the world; the earth trembled and quaked." The earth is moving, no question.

True. Verse 19 says, "Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found." God's way goes through the mighty waters, and His footprints weren't found. That's a mystery I love.

It's actually true, baker. Verse 19 says, "Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found." The path led through the sea, and the footprints were not to be found. That's just what the text says.

explanations.answer: Like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron
explanations.explanation: Verse 20 says, "You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron." Moses was Israel's leader, and Aaron was his brother (Exodus 4:14). A flock, friend, not a fancy parade. That's a gentle picture to end on.

explanations.answer: Like an army by the hand of Joshua and Caleb
explanations.explanation: Joshua and Caleb aren't named in this verse. Verse 20 says, "You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron." And the word is flock, not army. Moses was Israel's leader, and Aaron was with him.

explanations.answer: Like a nation by the hand of David and Solomon
explanations.explanation: David and Solomon aren't named in this verse. Verse 20 says, "You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron." Look at the picture, too: God leads them like a flock. Moses was Israel's leader, and Aaron is named right alongside him.
